problemText: Britain's early steam engines and iron furnaces ran on a fossil fuel that Britain happened to hold in shallow, abundant seams located near its iron deposits and its ports. Which fuel was it?
choices: Petroleum
Coal
Natural gas piped from Russia
Charcoal burned from domestic woodlands
hints: The fuel is the same one that filled mines with water — the problem the first steam engines were built to pump out.

problemText: During the 1700s, shared village fields across much of Britain were fenced off into privately owned farms, a process called enclosure. Why do historians treat enclosure as one of the preconditions for industrialization?
choices: It gave the government ownership of British farmland
It multiplied the number of guild-trained craft workshops in villages
It pushed rural laborers off the land, creating a pool of people who needed wage work just as mills needed hands
It ended Britain's need to trade with its overseas colonies
hints: Follow the displaced people, not the fences — where does someone with no field to work go for money?

problemText: The earliest textile mills had to be built beside fast-flowing rivers because the machinery was turned by water wheels. The improved steam engine of the later 1700s changed that constraint. What was the main consequence?
choices: Cloth production moved back into workers' cottages
Mills no longer needed large numbers of workers
Parliament outlawed the use of water power in manufacturing
Factories could be built wherever coal could be delivered, including in growing towns
hints: Ask what the river was supplying, and what the engine now supplied instead — then ask where a factory is free to stand.

problemText: The Stockton and Darlington railway opened in 1825, and within a few decades British goods that had once taken weeks to move overland arrived in days. Which outcome follows most directly from that change?
choices: Perishable food, mail, and daily newspapers could reach a genuinely national market
Long-distance shipping became more expensive than local hand carting
Britain's cities shrank as workers returned to rural villages
Regional price differences for goods grew steadily wider
hints: Ask which kinds of goods are ruined or worthless by a delay of weeks — those are the ones the railway newly made possible.

problemText: A physician surveying a northern English mill town wrote in 1845 (paraphrased): 'In this district the courts are unpaved and undrained, one privy serves some twenty houses, and families sleep in cellars below the level of the street.' Which feature of early industrial Britain does this account best document?
choices: The success of factory inspection in improving working conditions
The persistence of task-based work rhythms in the countryside
City populations growing far faster than housing, drainage, and clean water could be built for them
The decline of coal use in northern manufacturing towns
hints: The details are all about where people live and what happens to their waste and water — not about the factory floor.

problemText: Historians often warn that the phrase 'Industrial Revolution' is misleading. Which statement best captures why?
choices: It suggests a political uprising, when in fact the British monarchy was overthrown in the same period
It suggests a single event with an inventor and a date, when it was a rolling transformation lasting more than a century, spreading unevenly to Belgium, Germany, the United States, and Japan
It suggests change was slow, when in fact all British manufacturing converted to steam power within a single decade
It suggests the change was global, when in fact industrial production never spread beyond Britain
hints: Test the word 'revolution' against the timeline: how many decades separate the first spinning machines from the railway boom?
Then test it against the map: did every industrializing region start at the same moment?

problemText: In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published a short political pamphlet arguing that all recorded history has been a struggle between classes and that industry had reduced that struggle to owners versus workers. What is this pamphlet called?
choices: The Wealth of Nations
On the Origin of Species
The Communist Manifesto
The Ten Hours Act
hints: Two of the other titles are by different authors in different fields, and one is a law rather than a pamphlet.

problemText: A British writer argued in the 1840s that Parliament should set neither wages nor working hours, because markets left alone coordinate themselves through self-interest and any interference would only destroy jobs. Which position is he stating?
choices: Laissez-faire economic liberalism
Marxist socialism
Trade unionism
Reform legislation enforced by government inspectors
hints: The whole argument turns on what government should do — and his answer is 'nothing.' Match that to the label.

problemText: Trade unions in industrial Britain treated the strike as their ultimate source of leverage. Why did stopping work collectively give organized workers bargaining power that an individual worker did not have?
choices: Striking workers legally became part owners of the factory
The law required employers to raise wages whenever any worker complained
Individual workers owned the machines and could remove them from the mill
One worker could be replaced easily, but all of them stopping at once idled expensive machinery that cost the owner money every hour
hints: Compare what the owner loses when one hand quits with what the owner loses when the whole floor stops.

problemText: A British sanitary reformer argued in 1842 that filth and disease in the industrial cities were not merely a moral scandal but a financial drain, since sick and dying workers cost employers and local ratepayers money. Why was framing sanitation this way effective?
choices: It demonstrated that cholera was carried through foul air rather than water
It aimed the argument at the self-interest of property owners and taxpayers who had resisted purely moral appeals
It showed that epidemic disease struck only the poorest districts
It proved that public spending on sewers would be unnecessary
hints: Ask who had to be persuaded to approve the spending, and what kind of argument moves that particular audience.

problemText: A parliamentary committee reported in 1842 that children were working underground in British coal mines, hauling loads through passages too low for an adult to stand in. Within the same year Parliament barred women and young children from underground work. What does this sequence best illustrate?
choices: Investigation that made hidden conditions public could convert outrage into legislation
Parliament routinely passed laws first and investigated conditions afterward
The committee concluded that reports of mine conditions had been exaggerated
Parliament had taken ownership of Britain's coal mines
hints: Put the two events in order and ask what the report supplied that speeches had not.

problemText: A student claims that Britain's factory and mines acts were socialist measures, because anyone who wanted to help factory workers in the 1800s was a socialist. Which correction is most accurate?
choices: The acts were drafted by Marx and Engels and enacted by a workers' party
The acts transferred ownership of the mills and mines to the workers who ran them
The claim is correct, since reformers and socialists formed one movement with one program

The acts were written largely by reformers who accepted private ownership of industry and wanted to make it survivable, while socialists argued that relief granted from above leaves ownership untouched
hints: Sort the responses by what each one proposes to do with ownership of the factories — keep it or replace it.
A measure can be pro-worker and still be designed to stabilize the system it regulates.

problemText: Which statesman, serving as minister-president of Prussia, engineered German unification through wars against Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866, and France in 1870 and 1871?
choices: Camillo di Cavour
Giuseppe Garibaldi
Otto von Bismarck
Klemens von Metternich
hints: Two of these names belong to the Italian story, and one belongs to the Austrian conservative order of the 1810s through 1848.

problemText: A pamphlet circulating in Europe in the 1840s argues that people who share a language, a culture, and a history ought to govern themselves in one independent state, and that a ruling family's inherited claim to territory is no basis for legitimate government. Which idea is the pamphlet expressing?
choices: Nationalism
Absolutism
Feudalism
Mercantilism
hints: The pamphlet locates legitimacy in a people rather than in a dynasty — name the idea that makes that move.

problemText: After Western warships forced Japanese ports open, reformers overthrew the shogun in 1868, restored the emperor as a national symbol, and drove rapid industrialization and military modernization. What reasoning drove this program?
choices: Japan intended to restore the feudal authority of the regional lords
Japan had agreed by treaty to build factories under Western supervision
Japan planned to close its ports again and withdraw from all foreign contact
Japan's leaders concluded that a country must modernize quickly or risk being colonized as others had been
hints: Look at what Japan's leaders could see happening to China and to much of Asia at the same moment, and ask what lesson they drew.

problemText: In 1867 the Austrian Empire reorganized itself as Austria-Hungary, raising Hungarians to co-equal standing with Austrians under a shared monarch. Why did this arrangement fail to settle the empire's national tensions?
choices: Hungarians rejected the arrangement and immediately declared full independence
The empire's Czechs, Croats, Serbs, Poles, and Romanians received no comparable standing and pressed their own claims
The Compromise abolished the monarchy, leaving no government in place
Austria lost its industry in the settlement and could no longer pay its army
hints: Count the peoples living inside the empire, then count how many the deal actually promoted.

problemText: Napoleon's armies overran the German-speaking lands, abolished the centuries-old Holy Roman Empire in 1806, and consolidated hundreds of tiny states into a few dozen larger ones. How did a French conquest contribute to later German unification?
choices: Napoleon founded a united German state that survived his own defeat
French rule convinced German-speakers to adopt French national identity
It both simplified a fragmented map and provoked a shared German national feeling among people resisting foreign rule
It eliminated Prussia, clearing the way for a smaller Germany to form
hints: Track two separate effects of the occupation: what it did to the map, and what it did to how the occupied people thought of themselves.

problemText: In a region where several peoples live intermixed in the same towns and valleys, why does an ethnic understanding of nationhood tend to produce contested borders, while a civic understanding need not?
choices: Ethnic nationalism appeals only to industrial societies, and intermixed regions had no industry
Civic nationalism rejects the idea of independent states altogether, so no borders are ever drawn
Ethnic nationalism requires that every nation be ruled by a foreign monarch, which neighbors resist

Ethnic nationalism defines belonging by descent and language, so intermixed neighbors can never join the nation and must be ruled or removed, while civic nationalism defines belonging by shared citizenship and law, which newcomers can adopt
hints: Ask, for each version, what a person would have to do to become a member of the nation — and whether that is something a person can do at all.
Then apply the rule 'one people, one state' to a valley where three peoples live on the same street.

problemText: By 1914, European powers had brought nearly all of Africa under colonial rule. Which two African states remained independent?
choices: Egypt and Morocco
Ethiopia and Liberia
Sudan and Kenya
Ghana and South Africa
hints: One of the two had destroyed an invading European army in 1896; the other had been founded earlier in the century as a settlement for freed people from the United States.

problemText: By the 1890s Britain, France, Germany, Russia, and Japan each held exclusive economic privileges over railways, mines, and trade within a defined zone of China, even though China remained a sovereign country that was never formally annexed. What is such a zone called?
choices: A sphere of influence
A settler colony populated by European migrants
A formal colony annexed and governed by a European governor
A territory administered on behalf of an international organization
hints: The key detail is that no annexation took place — the foreign power took the profits without taking the flag.

problemText: The Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885 established, among the European powers, that a claim to African territory would count only if the claiming power actually placed administrators and officials on the ground. What effect did this rule have?
choices: It slowed European expansion by requiring the consent of African rulers
It guaranteed that new colonial borders would follow the boundaries of existing African kingdoms
It turned claim-staking into a physical race to occupy territory before a rival did
It made any line drawn on a map permanent, so no further expeditions were needed
hints: Ask what a power must now do the moment a rival announces a claim, and how fast it must do it.

problemText: A British colonial administrator wrote in 1893 (paraphrased): 'We bring courts, roads, and schools to peoples who, in our judgment, are not yet fit to govern themselves, and it is our duty to rule them until that day comes.' Which justification for empire is he offering?
choices: A nationalist argument that holding colonies proved a country's great-power status
An economic argument that colonies were needed as markets for surplus industrial goods
A strategic argument that colonies were needed as coaling stations to protect shipping routes
The civilizing mission — the assertion that Europeans had a duty to govern peoples they claimed were incapable of self-rule
hints: Nothing in the passage mentions money, rivals, or shipping — identify which of the era's justifications the words on the page actually make.

problemText: Britain built an extensive railway network across India during the later 1800s. Which statement best describes the purpose the network was designed and routed to serve?
choices: To give Indian manufacturers cheap access to inland customers
To move raw cotton, grain, and other materials from the interior out to the ports for export
To help Indian handloom weavers ship finished cloth to overseas buyers
To carry British settlers to farming colonies established in the interior
hints: Follow the direction of the track: if most lines run from inland districts to a seaport, what is moving, and which way?

problemText: Ethiopia under Menelik II destroyed an invading Italian army at Adwa in 1896 and kept its independence, and Zulu forces wiped out a British column at Isandlwana in 1879 before being overwhelmed. Which conclusion do these outcomes best support?
choices: African conquest succeeded through a gap in firepower and industrial resupply and through European exploitation of rivalries between African states, not through African passivity — organized African states could and sometimes did win
African resistance to European conquest was rare, and Adwa was the only battle Africans ever fought
Ethiopia stayed independent because the European powers had agreed at Berlin to respect its sovereignty
European armies held no technological advantage anywhere in Africa
hints: Start from the fact that these were pitched battles between organized states, and ask what that rules out about the usual story.
Then ask why victories like these were the exception rather than the rule — what could a European force replace after a defeat that an African force could not?
